extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent prosecutors and practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent application's specification satisfies the enablement requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA) / 112(a), including how examiners should assess evidence, claim scope, examples, predictability, and burden of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement — make and use without undue experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A conclusion of lack of enablement means that, based on the evidence regarding each of the enablement factors, the specification, at the time the application was filed, would not have taught one skilled in the art how to make and/or use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination is reached by weighing all factual considerations (Wands factors). The examiner must consider relevant evidence as a whole and base any nonenablement conclusion on that evidence. Citations: In re Wright; In re Wands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of all Wands factual factors together
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper to conclude a disclosure is not enabling based on analysis of only one factor while ignoring one or more of the others; the examiner’s analysis must consider all evidence related to each factor and conclusions must be based on the evidence as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not necessary to discuss each factor in every rejection, the rejection explanation should focus on the factors, reasons, and evidence leading to nonenablement, with specific factual findings supported by evidence. See In re Wands, In re Marzocchi; references to MPEP §§2164.08, 2164.05(a), 2164.05(b), 2164.03, 2164.02, 2164.06.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to make the claimed invention — one method may suffice if correlated
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification discloses at least one method for making and using the claimed invention that bears a reasonable correlation to the entire scope of the claim, the enablement requirement is satisfied; failure to disclose other methods does not render the claim invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For unstable/transitory intermediates, the applicant need not teach how to make a stable or isolatable form. The availability of starting materials or apparatus is a key issue—if a required apparatus or chemical is not readily available, sufficient disclosure of it is required. Cases: In re Fisher; In re Breslow; In re Ghiron; In re Howarth.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to use the claimed invention — known modes and dosage
rubrics_metrics.description: If a statement of utility connotes how to use and the art recognizes standard modes of administration, 35 U.S.C. 112 is satisfied. Dosage or method of use need not be specified if one skilled in the art could obtain such information without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a claim is limited by a particular use, enablement is evaluated based on that limitation. If multiple uses are disclosed and at least one is enabled, the specification may be enabling for the claimed invention. Cases: In re Johnson; In re Hitchings; In re Brana; In re Vaeck.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working examples — presence, prophetic examples, and weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance with enablement does not turn on whether an example is disclosed. Examples may be working (based on performed work) or prophetic (based on predicted results). The specification need not contain an example if the disclosure otherwise enables without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of a working example is a factor to be considered, especially in unpredictable arts, but should never be the sole reason for rejecting a claim. A single working example can preclude a rejection stating nothing is enabled, though the presence of only one working example can be a factor in assessing whether the claimed scope is broader than enabled. Cases: Gould v. Quigg; Re Borkowski; Re Brana.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation between in vitro/in vivo models and claimed uses
rubrics_metrics.description: An in vitro or in vivo animal model example constitutes a working example only if it 'correlates' with a disclosed or claimed method of use; lack of correlation means the example does not constitute a working example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a model correlates depends on the state of the prior art; if a model is recognized to correlate, it should be accepted unless the examiner has evidence it does not. Examiner bears initial burden to give reasons for lack of correlation and must weigh evidence for and against correlation. Rigorous exact correlation is not required if probative evidence supports reasonable correlation. Case: In re Brana; Cross v. Iizuka.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed genus — representative examples and genus-wide enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: For a claimed genus, representative examples together with a statement applicable to the genus may ordinarily be sufficient if one skilled in the art would expect the genus could be used without undue experimentation. Proof of enablement for other members of the genus is required only when adequate reasons are advanced to show inability to extrapolate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must provide adequate reasons if asserting a genus is not enabled. See MPEP §2164.02(III).

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability of the art vs. amount of guidance required
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of guidance or direction needed in the specification is inversely related to what is known in the prior art and the predictability in the art; nascent or unpredictable technologies require more specific and useful teaching to be enabling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In unpredictable arts (e.g., many chemical reactions, physiological activity), disclosure of a single species usually will not support broad genus claims; in predictable arts (mechanical, electrical), a single embodiment may provide broad enablement. Cite: In re Fisher; In re Marzocchi; In re Vickers; In re Soll; Chiron v. Genentech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on the examiner to establish a reasonable basis for nonenablement
rubrics_metrics.description: Before analyzing enablement, the examiner must construe the claims and select meanings for ambiguous terms; to make a rejection, the examiner has the initial burden to establish a reasonable basis to question enablement and explain why the disclosure is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must explain why it doubts the truth or accuracy of supporting disclosure and back up assertions with acceptable evidence or reasoning. Minimal requirement per In re Bowen: give reasons explaining uncertainty. Examiners should present the best case in the first Office action and identify enabled allowable subject matter early (compact prosecution principles). Cases: Genentech v. Wellcome; In re Wright; In re Marzocchi; In re Bowen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement determination must be based on the evidence as a whole — no personal opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must weigh all evidence—specification, applicant submissions (declarations, affidavits, references), and evidence/reasoning presented in the rejection—and decide if the claimed invention is enabled based on the weight of the record, not personal opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may submit declarations under 37 C.F.R. 1.132 or cite references; such evidence must be commensurate with the specification and the claimed scope. Declarations and submissions carry weight proportionate to factual support they provide. Cases: In re Brandstadter; In re Buchner; In re Alton.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must be enabling as of the filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the specification would have been enabling as of the filing date involves consideration of the nature of the invention, the state of the prior art at filing, and the level of skill in the art at that time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The state of the art is assessed as of the filing date; post-filing publications generally cannot be used to show what was known at filing, except to the extent they evidence what skilled artisans would have known. The pertinent art should be defined in terms of the problem to be solved. Cases: Chiron v. Genentech; In re Gunn; In re Budnick; In re Wright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must be enabling to persons skilled in each relevant art
rubrics_metrics.description: Where different arts are involved, the specification is enabling if it enables persons skilled in each art to carry out the aspect applicable to their specialty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two distinct technologies are relevant, disclosure is adequate if a person of ordinary skill in each technology could practice the invention from the disclosure (e.g., computer art cooperating with fuel injection art). Cases: In re Naquin; Technicon Instruments; Ex parte Zechnall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of experimentation — routine vs. undue
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantity of experimentation needed is one factor in determining 'undue experimentation.' Extended experimentation may not be undue if sufficient direction is provided; the test is not merely quantitative—routine experimentation is permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time and expense are factors but not determinative. In chemical arts, difficulty of assays and guidance for carrying them out bear on quantity. Examples: United States v. Telectronics (reasonable experimentation despite time/cost); In re Ghiron (functional block diagrams insufficient because required extensive development).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of missing information — identify essential missing elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Doubt about enablement often arises because information is missing about one or more essential claim elements or relationships which a skilled person could not develop without undue experimentation; examiner should specifically identify what is missing and why it is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting missing information, examiner should explain how the missing data prevents enabling the full claim scope and supply references if possible to support a prima facie case. See MPEP §2164.06(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Electrical/mechanical claims and broad claim language risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement serves to prevent claims broader than the disclosed invention. Broad claim language is used at the peril of losing claims that cannot be enabled across the full scope—lack of details for embodiments (e.g., electronic sensors) can render claims nonenabled for those embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include claims that cover mechanical and electronic embodiments where specification lacks disclosure for one type (e.g., electronic side impact sensors) — the specification must apprise how to make and use such embodiments or claims may fail enablement. Cases: MagSil Corp. v. Hitachi; Auto. Techs. Int'l, Inc. v. BMW.

rubrics_metrics.name: Starting materials/apparatus availability requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If practice of a method requires a particular apparatus or starting materials, the application must provide sufficient disclosure of the apparatus or materials if they are not readily available to one skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is particularly important in biotechnology when a required microorganism or strain is only obtainable after extensive screening; if needed apparatus/chemicals are not readily available, adequate disclosure is required. Case: In re Ghiron; In re Howarth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of post-filing references to show nonenablement — limited exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, examiners should not use post-filing date references to demonstrate a patent is not enabled; exceptions exist if a later reference provides evidence of what one skilled in the art would have known on or before the effective filing date or shows impossibility at filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A later publication may support a nonenablement position if it demonstrates that the invention was not possible at the time of filing. Examiner may consider later evidence as indirect proof of prior lack of enablement in appropriate circumstances. Cases: In re Hogan; In re Wright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight and sufficiency of applicant-submitted evidence (declarations, FDA submissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may submit declarations, affidavits, or regulatory submissions to rebut a prima facie case of lack of enablement; such evidence must convincingly show that one skilled in the art could make and use the claimed invention at the filing date and must be commensurate with the claimed scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should compare steps, materials, and conditions in applicant's evidence with those in the application to ensure they are commensurate in scope and were supported by the specification as filed and what was well-known at filing. FDA submissions may be considered but their standards differ from USPTO enablement requirements. Cases: In re Brandstadter; Scott v. Finney; In re Alton; In re Buchner.
